speculation

/spek-yuh-LAY-shun/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Speculation means the forming of theories or guesses about something without firm evidence.

Weeks of speculation about which astronaut would command the mission ended only when the agency released its crew list.

Example

When the star quarterback skipped practice twice in one week, the hallways filled with speculation — some said he was injured, others said he was transferring, but nobody actually knew anything.

Everyone is building theories — injury, transfer — while the sentence tells us plainly that nobody has any real information. Theories multiplying in the absence of evidence is exactly what speculation is.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

conjecture: A conjecture is a single opinion or explanation formed without proof — one candidate answer put forward. Speculation is the wider activity of theorizing without firm evidence, and one afternoon of speculation can produce a dozen conjectures. Conjecture names the guess; speculation names the guessing.

guesswork: Guesswork is the process of making guesses, often blind ones with nothing behind them — filling in answers at random is guesswork. Speculation is more ambitious: it builds whole theories and explanations, reasoning past the evidence rather than merely picking blindly. Guesswork stabs; speculation constructs.

supposition: A supposition is something quietly assumed to be true without proof — a premise slipped into the reasoning. Speculation is louder and more active: openly floating theories about what might be true. A supposition hides underneath an argument; speculation does its guessing out in the open.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

certainty: the state of being completely sure, beyond doubt

fact: something known to be true

Where it sits · how far the mind outruns the evidence — wondering → speculation → fantasy

wondering vs. speculation: Wondering is idle and open — you're just musing, with no theory in mind; speculation actively builds explanations even though the evidence isn't there.

fantasy vs. speculation: Fantasy goes further than speculation — it lets go of evidence entirely and imagines freely, with no expectation of being true at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — specul-

Root — specul-: to spy out, observe from a watchtower (Latin speculari, from specere 'to look at')

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: act or result of

Put it together

Put it together: Speculation began as 'keeping watch from a lookout' — scanning the horizon for what might come. The Latin root specere means 'to look at,' and today speculation means mentally scanning the possibilities when solid evidence isn't in view.

Use the root in a new word: spectacle

Use the root in a new word: spectacle: A spectacle is something striking to look at — the fireworks finale over the bay was a spectacle the whole town came out to see.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Neutral / Journalistic

Speculation often travels with dismissive partners: 'pure speculation,' 'mere speculation,' 'idle speculation' — phrases writers use to wave away unproven claims. SAT reading passages also use its finance sense: risky investing based on guesses about future prices. Keep it distinct from prediction: a prediction is a committed, stated forecast (often evidence-based); speculation is open guessing with little or no evidence.
